title: The stories we tell | SEND
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart argues that school leaders should use storytelling to build staff's collective understanding of special educational needs provision, drawing on Daniel Willingham's point that stories are psychologically privileged and Daniel Coyle's advice to 'fill the windscreen with stories'. He structures the SEND story around the features of narrative: conflict (the school's dominant areas of need), causality (the universal provision chosen to address them), complications (targeted interventions) and character (children who are flourishing). A key trap, he says, is telling the intervention story before the universal-provision story, because classroom teaching has the greatest impact and the aim is to shift staff beliefs that high-quality teaching is the first layer and every teacher owns every child's progress. He illustrates with universal strategies such as teaching with memory in mind, a mastery model, scaffolding and language and emotion-regulation routines, and with carefully chosen interventions linked tightly to classroom practice. Success stories about individual children let staff attribute progress to these approaches. He concludes that leaders need deep knowledge of the school's SEND profile to tell these stories well, and should tell them often and refine them.
points: Stories are easier to understand and remember, so leaders can use them to build shared mental models of SEND provision that drive staff behaviour.
Hart maps the SEND narrative onto conflict, causality, complications and character: need, universal provision, intervention and success stories.
Tell the universal-provision story before the intervention story, since everyday classroom teaching has the greatest impact and the goal is to align beliefs about it.
Interventions only work when their strategies carry into the classroom and the class teacher actively uses the same language and approaches.
Celebrating specific children's progress and attributing it to the chosen strategies helps colleagues adopt the underlying beliefs.
quotes: If we want colleagues to understand and remember our message in order to influence their behaviour, telling stories appears an effective way of doing so.

There is one particular trap to avoid and that is telling the story of intervention before telling the story of universal provision. The first reason for this is that it is what happens in the classroom on a day to day basis that will have the greatest impact on learning.

And a key belief in the provision for SEND is that high quality teaching is the first layer of provision to get right and that all teachers are responsible for the progress of all children in their class.
We reject the conveyor belt model where lessons and units of work move on regardless of whether children have understood. Instead, we check understanding regularly and adapt our practice.

The strength of an intervention lies in the application of its strategies in day to day situations in the classroom and for this to work, there is a great deal of communication between the person running the intervention and the class teacher.
For colleagues to adopt a new underlying belief (for example any of the detail above), they need to attribute success to those ways of working.
Story tellers get better with each iteration and so if colleagues need to understand SEND provision and school leaders want to influence behaviour, these stories need to be told often.
